{{Short description|Infinite series summable to 1/3}}
[[Image:Halfminusquarter.png|frame|right|Demonstration that {{sfrac|1|2}} − {{sfrac|1|4}} + {{sfrac|1|8}} − {{sfrac|1|16}} + ⋯ = {{sfrac|1|3}}]]

In [[mathematics]], the [[infinite series]] {{nowrap|1/2 − 1/4 + 1/8 − 1/16 + ⋯}}
is a simple example of an [[alternating series]] that [[absolute convergence|converges absolutely]].

It is a [[geometric series]] whose first term is {{sfrac|1|2}} and whose common ratio is −{{sfrac|1|2}}, so its sum is
:<math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2^n}=\frac12-\frac14+\frac18-\frac{1}{16}+\cdots=\frac{\frac12}{1-(-\frac12)} = \frac13.</math>

==Hackenbush and the surreals==
[[Image:Hackenbush two thirds.svg|frame|right|Demonstration of {{sfrac|2|3}} via a zero-value game]]
A slight rearrangement of the series reads
:<math>1-\frac12-\frac14+\frac18-\frac{1}{16}+\cdots=\frac13.</math>

The series has the form of a positive integer plus a series containing every negative [[power of two]] with either a positive or negative sign, so it can be translated into the infinite blue-red [[Hackenbush]] string that represents the [[surreal number]] {{sfrac|1|3}}:
:LRRLRLR... = {{sfrac|1|3}}.{{sfn|Berlekamp|Conway|Guy|1982|p=79}}

A slightly simpler Hackenbush string eliminates the repeated R:
:LRLRLRL... = {{sfrac|2|3}}.{{sfn|Berlekamp|Conway|Guy|1982|pp=307–308}}

In terms of the Hackenbush game structure, this equation means that the board depicted on the right has a value of 0; whichever player moves second has a winning strategy.

==Related series==
*The statement that {{nowrap|{{sfrac|1|2}} − {{sfrac|1|4}} + {{sfrac|1|8}} − {{sfrac|1|16}} + ⋯}} is absolutely convergent means that the series {{nowrap|[[1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 + ⋯|{{sfrac|1|2}} + {{sfrac|1|4}} + {{sfrac|1|8}} + {{sfrac|1|16}} + ⋯]]}} is convergent. In fact, the latter series converges to [[1 (number)|1]], and it proves that one of the [[binary expansion]]s of 1 is 0.111....
*Pairing up the terms of the series {{nowrap|{{sfrac|1|2}} − {{sfrac|1|4}} + {{sfrac|1|8}} − {{sfrac|1|16}} + ⋯}} results in another geometric series with the same sum, {{nowrap|[[1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + 1/256 + ⋯|{{sfrac|1|4}} + {{sfrac|1|16}} + {{sfrac|1|64}} + {{sfrac|1|256}} + ⋯]]}}. This series is one of the first to be summed in the [[history of mathematics]]; it was used by [[Archimedes]] circa 250–200&nbsp;BC.{{sfn|Shawyer|Watson|1994|p=3}}
*The [[Euler transform]] of the divergent series {{nowrap|[[1 − 2 + 4 − 8 + ⋯]]}} is {{nowrap|{{sfrac|1|2}} − {{sfrac|1|4}} + {{sfrac|1|8}} − {{sfrac|1|16}} + ⋯}}. Therefore, even though the former series does not have a sum in the usual sense, it is [[Euler summation|Euler summable]] to {{sfrac|1|3}}.{{sfn|Korevaar |2004|p=325}}
